newsitem.title: FRANCE: French oil refinery strike drags into second week.
newsitem.headline: French oil refinery strike drags into second week.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe's strike-weary government received slight relief on Thursday when airline pilots called off a stoppage, but action elsewhere hit oil refineries, transport and also threatened post offices.
A refinery strike at oil giant Elf Aquitaine went into a second week amid union calls for a nationwide protest to save oil industry jobs.

However, a spokesman for the airline pilots' union said a two-day strike slated for December 10-11 had been called off. This followed signs of a possible breakthrough in a long-running labour conflict on job contracts.
The strike over 330 job cuts at Elf, France's largest oil firm, crippled a quarter of the country's refining output for an eighth day on Thursday with few if any signs of it melting.
Unions and management were due to meet on Thursday afternoon over pay and conditions which Elf says it is willing to discuss.
But union leaders said they would refuse to negotiate about pay and demand the full withdrawal of the job cuts plan before starting on other issues like pay and early retirement.
"We want to talk about jobs and how Elf should be hiring people not firing them," said one union official beforehand.
Elf officials have said the job reductions are necessary and cannot be negotiated.
In other French disputes, striking bus drivers paralysed services in the southern city of Toulouse for the third day on Thursday over early retirement.
Public transport in Lyon, France's second city, was reduced in a protest over recent assaults on bus drivers.
Meanwhile, the Communist-backed CGT union canvassed support for a week of action at post offices from December 9 to protest about partial privatisation plans.

The industrial action has been partly inspired by concessions to striking truck drivers, who gained a cut in the retirement age to 55 from 60 for drivers with 25 years' experience. The truckers' 12-day strike ended on Friday.

Inside the stricken Elf refineries, some workers were at odds with their own unions. They quarrelled with a deal to allow some products out of Elf's three French refineries for one day from Thursday in return for the opening of talks.

"Some of our guys are saying it will just give the company a chance to fill up its depots again or get everything out by tanker," said a union official at the coastal Donges refinery in western France, the country's biggest oil plant.
The week-old strike has caused a huge logistical problem for Elf and helped to drive up international gasoline prices.
But its impact has been slow to get through to ordinary consumers, in part because of the blockade of depots by the French truckers last month, which kept most tanks full.
Unions now hope to spread disruption across the French oil industry with a nationwide strike on December 10.
A strike would affect an eighth of European oil refining capacity, but both oil company and union officials said full participation in all 13 French refineries was not yet certain.
Unions accuse oil firms -- among them Elf and Total and foreign oil giants like Esso, Shell, Mobil and BP -- of trying to axe at least 1,500 jobs this year without economic reason.
Oil companies say Europe is confronted by a glut of spare refining capacity and restructuring cannot be avoided.
